div.p: Objective: Although awake craniotomy can guide functional brain mapping and resection, its feasibility and safety have been poorly studied in large series of patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy surgery.

div.head: Methods:
div.p: We conducted an observational, retrospective, single-center cohort study of 588 consecutive awake craniotomies (2010-2024). Patients with drugresistant focal epilepsy were compared to controls, with a focus on subgroup analysis of patients with low-grade, developmental, epilepsy-associated brain tumor and an associated nontumoral epileptogenic brain lesion group (46/558 patients, 8.2%), patients with ≥2 years of uncontrolled epileptic seizures (32/558 patients, 5.6%), and patients on ≥2 antiseizure medications (77/588 patients, 13.1%). Feasibility outcomes included time to awakening, intraoperative cooperation, and procedure abortion. Safety outcomes included surgery-related risks and intraoperative and early postoperative epileptic seizures.

Results: Compared to controls, patients with medically drug-resistant focal epilepsy (1) did not present higher rates of late awakening (6.5%-14.3% vs. 8.7%-9.8%, p = .450, p = .972, p = .143) or of insufficient intraoperative cooperation (0%-9.1% vs. 5.0%-6.1%, p = .019, p = .345, p = .173), (2) did not require abortion of the awake procedure because of epilepsy (0% vs. 0%, p = 1.0), (3) did not present a higher rate of intraoperative epileptic seizures (4.3%-9.1% vs. 2.7%-5.0%, p = .226, p = .529), (4) presented a higher rate of intraoperative epileptic seizures when presenting a ≥2year history of uncontrolled epileptic seizures (12.9% vs. 2.3%, p < .001), and (5) did not exhibit a higher rate of early postoperative epileptic seizures (13.0%-19.3% vs. 9.8%-10.6%, p = .613, p = .143, p = .078). div.head: | I N T RO DUCTI ON
div.p: Awake craniotomy is the current gold standard for surgical treatment of brain tumors located within eloquent brain areas, as it optimizes both safety and resection rates. [1][2][3] This approach has also been proposed for drug-resistant focal epilepsy (DRFE) when the epileptogenic zone lies within or adjacent to eloquent brain areas. [4][5][6] In these patients, identifying essential eloquent brain areas during preoperative workup, including during stereoelectroencephalography with cortical electrical stimulations or by using functional magnetic resonance imaging, may be challenging, and there may be partial overlap between eloquent brain areas and the epileptogenic zone. 7 Intraoperative functional brain mapping under awake conditions may therefore enable tailored resections of epileptogenic tissue within eloquent areas, without inducing permanent deficits as demonstrated for glioma surgery. 6 Although awake craniotomy for functional brain mapping during DRFE surgery may be valuable, its feasibility and safety are poorly studied. 8,9 In particular, the occurrence of perioperative epileptic seizures is a potential concern in DRFE patients, and intraoperative epileptic seizures may impact the functional brain mapping and, subsequently, the resection. The impact of DRFE-related factors, such as seizure control, duration of epilepsy, and antiseizure medication, on the conduction of the awake procedure remains to be addressed.

Here, we assessed feasibility (including time to awakening, intraoperative cooperation, and procedure abortion) and safety (including surgery-related risks and intraoperative seizures) of awake craniotomy for patients with DRFE.

div.head: | M AT E RIALS AND M ETHODS
| Study design and setting
div.p: We conducted an observational, retrospective, cohort study conducted at a tertiary referral neurosurgical epilepsy center between January 2010 and December 2024. The study received required authorizations (A01933-48) from the human research institutional review board (CPP Sud Est 12017-35). Written informed consent was obtained for all participants. The manuscript was written in accordance with the STROBE (Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology) guidelines. 10

div.head: | Participants
div.p: Inclusion criteria were (1) resection of a brain lesion with intraoperative functional brain mapping using direct electrical stimulation in the awake condition and (2) available preoperative epilepsy status. Patients with incomplete clinical data were excluded. The study included 558 consecutive patients, corresponding to all eligible patients during the study period. procedure abortion, or occurrence of intraoperative or early postoperative epileptic seizures.

Significance: Awake craniotomy appears feasible and safe in patients with medically drug-resistant focal epilepsy, with similar and low rates of adverse events, including intraoperative epileptic seizures.

div.head: K E Y W O R D S
div.p: awake surgery, drug-resistant focal epilepsy, feasibility, safety

div.head: Key points
div.p: • The feasibility and safety of awake craniotomy have been poorly studied in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. • Patients with medically drug-resistant focal epilepsy did not present higher rates of late awakening, of insufficient intraoperative cooperation, or of intraoperative epileptic seizures. • In multivariable analysis, drug-resistant focal epilepsy was not independently associated with time to awakening, intraoperative cooperation, procedure abortion, or occurrence of intraoperative or early postoperative epileptic seizures.
• Awake craniotomy appears feasible and safe in patients with medically drug-resistant focal epilepsy.

div.head: | Data collection
div.p: Variables were collected from medical records using a pseudonymized and standardized form. Variables included sex, age, handedness, presenting symptoms, history of epileptic seizure (duration, seizure control, number of antiseizure medications), Karnofsky Performance Scale score, histomolecular diagnosis, duration of the awake phase of the surgery, current intensity used for intraoperative brain mapping, intraoperative adverse events (epileptic seizure, time to awakening, insufficient intraoperative cooperation, awake craniotomy abortion), early postoperative epileptic seizures, hospital stay duration, and mode of discharge. Epileptic seizure types were classified according to the International League Against Epilepsy. 11 Epileptic seizure control was defined as a patient completely free of any epileptic seizure with or without ongoing antiseizure medication. 12 Slow awakening was defined as a time interval of ≥30 min between discontinuation of sedative agents (stopped at dura mater opening in all patients) and the start of awake functional mapping with a cooperative and fully conscious patient. 1 Insufficient intraoperative cooperation was evaluated by the surgical team and defined as a patient's inability to reliably perform efficient neurological, language, and/or neurocognitive intraoperative tasks for any reason during the whole duration of the awake phase, regardless of the underlying cause. 1 The Awake Surgery Intraoperative Cooperation (ASIC) score was measured as previously reported. 1

div.head: | Surgical procedure
div.p: All awake surgeries were performed by the same neurosurgeon using a standardized "asleep-awakeasleep" protocol previously detailed. 1,3,13,14 On the day of the surgery, no anxiolytic or sedative medication were given, and antiseizure medications were maintained as usual on an individual basis. A forced-air heating blanket maintained the patient's body temperature above 36°C. Total intravenous general anesthesia was induced using propofol and remifentanil. Pressure-controlled ventilation with a laryngeal mask airway ensured normocapnia. Intravenous antiemetics, analgesics, antibiotic prophylaxis, steroids, and an intravenous loading dose of levetiracetam (500 mg) were systematically administered at induction whatever the regular antiseizure medication.

Functional mapping was conducted by direct electrical stimulation (bipolar electrode, 5-mm distance between tips, 60-Hz stimulation frequency; biphasic current, 1-ms phase duration; 4-s stimulation duration; Osiris NeuroStimulator, Inomed). Electrophysiological monitoring using electrocorticography (bipolar recordings, four-to eight-contact cortical electrode; DIXI Medical) was performed systematically in DRFE patients (but not in diffuse glioma patients) to help identify epileptogenic tissue by dynamically recording interictal epileptiform discharges from the exposed cortex and to guide surgical decision-making, implying the electrode to by placed and removed throughout the resection. Intraoperative epileptic seizures were recorded on a clinical basis. The cortical mapping began by stimulating the sensory/motor area to identify the lowest current threshold inducing reproducible positive responses (baseline at 1 mA with .5-mA increments). The same current intensity served for further mapping; the exposed brain was tested, and all sites were stimulated at least three times to confirm reproducibility. To control for neurological and cognitive functions, intraoperative tasks were performed according to practical guidelines. 14,15 The types of disturbances were classified by a senior speech therapist. Sites inducing a functional impairment were marked with sterile numbered tags and considered eloquent. The lesion was resected using subpial dissection and aspiration, combined with continuous subcortical functional mapping in an awake patient performing the required tasks. Resection was stopped when eloquent subcortical structures were encountered within the surgical cavity with no security margin left around the functional connectivity. Residual lesional tissue in noneloquent areas was removed under general anesthesia once the awake phase was complete. The management of intraoperative epileptic seizures followed a standardized protocol, as previously reported. 13 Upon clinical detection of an intraoperative epileptic seizure, direct electrical stimulation was immediately stopped, and the brain was irrigated with cold (4-8°C) normal saline solution (.9% NaCl) until seizure resolution. No systemic anticonvulsant was administered. Surgery resumed as soon as the patient regained the ability to perform intraoperative tasks.

div.head: | Statistical analysis
div.p: We assessed the feasibility and safety of awake craniotomy in patients with DRFE, focusing our analysis on three subgroups: (1) patients with low-grade, developmental, epilepsy-associated brain tumor (LEAT) and associated nontumoral epileptogenic brain lesion; (2) patients with ≥2year history of uncontrolled epileptic seizures; and (3) patients with ≥2 antiseizure medications. Each subgroup was compared to a corresponding control group comprising the rest of the patients of the cohort, that is, without the subgroup feature. Descriptive statistics were reported as the mean ± SD for continuous variables and as numbers and percentages for categorical variables. Univariate comparisons were carried out using chi-squared or Fisher exact test for comparing categorical variables and one-way analysis of variance or Kruskal-Wallis test for continuous variable, as appropriate.

In addition, we assessed the predictors associated with time to awakening, intraoperative cooperation, procedure abortion, and the occurrence of intraoperative and of early postoperative epileptic seizures. Univariable analyses were conducted to calculate unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) for each potential predictor. Variables demonstrating an association with the outcome of interest at a significance level of p < .100 in the univariable analysis were subsequently included in multivariable logistic regression models. A backward stepwise selection approach was applied to identify independent predictors, retaining variables with statistical significance in the final model.
A two-tailed p-value < .05 was considered statistically significant. Analyses were performed using JMP Pro software (version 18.0.2, SAS Institute). 3 | R E S U LTS

div.head: | Study population
div.p: A total of 558 patients were included (53.2% men, mean 42 ± 14 years old). Characteristics of the study population are summarized in Table 1.

The LEAT group included 46 of 558 patients (8.2%) presenting with an LEAT or with an associated nontumoral epileptogenic brain lesion. These included gangliogliomas (n = 17), focal cortical dysplasias (n = 9), dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors (n = 5), angiocentric gliomas (n = 3), papillary glioneuronal tumors (n = 2), pilocytic astrocytomas (n = 2), cysts (n = 2), posttraumatic scars (n = 2), diffuse astrocytoma, MYBL1-altered glioma (n = 1), ulegyria, (n = 1), postinfection scar (n = 1), and meningioangiomatosis (n = 1). They were compared to the other 512 patients.

The uncontrolled epilepsy group comprised 32 of 558 patients (5.6%) presenting with a ≥2year history of uncontrolled focal epileptic seizures. These included focal cortical dysplasias (n = 8), IDH-mutant astrocytomas (n = 7), IDH-mutant and 1p19q-codeleted oligodendrogliomas (n = 6), gangliogliomas (n = 3), dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumors (n = 2), cavernous angiomas (n = 2), a pleomorphic xanthoastrocytoma (n = 1), ulegyria (n = 1), and meningioangiomatosis (n = 1). They were compared to the other 527 patients.

Intraoperatively, compared to the control group, patients of the LEAT group did not present a higher rate of late awakening (6.5% vs. 9.8%, p = .450) and did not present a higher rate of intraoperative seizure (4.3% vs. 2.7%, p = .529) despite on average a higher current intensity having been used for intraoperative functional brain mapping (mean = 3.7 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1 mA, p = .011). No awake procedure was aborted, and no surgical strategy was modified in either group (0% vs. 0%, p = 1.0). Notably, patients of the LEAT group had a lower rate of insufficient intraoperative cooperation (0% vs. 6.1%, p = .019). Postoperatively, patients of the LEAT group did not present a higher rate of early postoperative epileptic seizures (13.0% vs. 10.6%, p = .613). Duration of hospital stay and mode of discharge were similar.

In multivariable analysis, the low-grade, developmental, epilepsy-associated brain tumor and associated nontumoral epileptogenic brain lesion parameter was not independently associated with time to awakening, intraoperative cooperation, procedure abortion, or occurrence of intraoperative or early postoperative epileptic seizures.

div.head: | Awake craniotomy in patients with a ≥2year history of uncontrolled epileptic seizures
div.p: Comparative analyses are detailed in Table 3. Compared to the control group, patients of the uncontrolled epilepsy group were younger (mean = 31 ± 12 vs. 44 ± 14 years old, p < .001) and presented more frequently with epileptic seizures as initial symptom (87.1% vs. 62.4%, p = .015); all had a history of epilepsy at the time of surgery (100% vs. 67.7%, p < .001) and per se of ongoing uncontrolled epileptic seizures (100% vs. 16.5%, p < .001); and they had a longer epilepsy duration (mean = 136 ± 95 vs. 9 ± 28 months, p < .001). Intraoperatively, compared to the control group, patients of the uncontrolled epilepsy group did not present a higher rate of late awakening (9.7% vs. 9.5%, p = .972) or insufficient intraoperative cooperation (9.7% vs. 5.4%, p = .345). However, they exhibited a higher rate of intraoperative seizure (12.9% vs. 2.3%, p < .001) despite on average similar current intensity used for intraoperative functional brain mapping (mean = 3.6 ± 1.4 vs. 3.3 ± 1.1 mA, p = .472). No awake procedure was aborted, and no surgical strategy was modified in either group (0% vs. 0%, p = 1.0). Postoperatively, compared to the control group, patients of the uncontrolled epilepsy group did not present a higher rate of early postoperative epileptic seizures (19.3% vs. 10.3%, p = .143). Duration of hospital stay and mode of discharge were similar.

In multivariable analysis, the ≥2year history of uncontrolled epileptic seizures parameter was not independently associated with time to awakening, intraoperative cooperation, procedure abortion, or occurrence of early postoperative epileptic seizures but was independently associated with intraoperative epileptic seizures (adjusted OR = 7.22, 95% confidence interval = 1.41-35.9, p = .017).

div.head: ≥2 antiseizure medications at the time of surgery
div.p: Comparative analyses are detailed in Table 4. Compared to the control group, patients of the ≥2 antiseizure medications group presented with epileptic seizures as initial symptom more frequently (90.9% vs. 59.5%, p < .001), had by definition a higher prevalence of epilepsy at surgery (100% vs. 65.1%, p < .001), more likely had uncontrolled epileptic seizures at surgery (60.0% vs. 14.4%, p < .001), and had a longer duration of epilepsy (mean = 62 ± 89 vs. 11 ± 31 months, p < .001). Intraoperatively, compared to the control group, patients of the ≥2 antiseizure medications group did not present a higher rate of late awakening (14.3% vs. 8.7%, p = .143) or insufficient intraoperative cooperation (9.1% vs. 5.0%, p = .173). Patients did not present a higher rate of intraoperative seizures (9.1% vs. 5.0%, p = .226), despite on average higher current intensity having been used for intraoperative functional brain mapping (mean = 3.6 ± 1.2 vs. 3.2 ± 1.1 mA, p = .004). No awake procedure was aborted, and no surgical strategy was modified in either group (0% vs. 0%, p = 1.0). Postoperatively, compared to the control group, patients of the ≥2 antiseizure medications group did not present a higher rate of early postoperative epileptic seizures (16.9% vs. 9.8%, p = .078). They presented a longer duration of hospital stay (mean 11 ± 16 vs. 9 ± 11 days, p = .022) and were less frequently discharged at home (79.0% vs. 89.4%, p = .037).

In multivariable analysis, the ≥2 antiseizure medications parameter was not independently associated with time to awakening, intraoperative cooperation, procedure abortion, or occurrence of intraoperative and early postoperative epileptic seizures.

div.head: | Key results
div.p: In this retrospective single-center cohort study of 558 consecutive awake craniotomies, patients with DRFE demonstrated comparable feasibility and safety outcomes compared to control patients. Specifically, these patients did not present higher rates of late awakening, insufficient intraoperative cooperation, or abortion of the awake procedure because of epilepsy. The occurrence of intraoperative seizures was not increased in the LEAT or ≥2 antiseizure medication subgroups. However, patients with a ≥2year history of uncontrolled seizure at the time of surgery exhibited a significantly higher rate of intraoperative epileptic seizures without interfering with the procedure. Early postoperative seizure rates did not differ across groups.

div.head: | Interpretation
div.p: We assessed the feasibility and safety of awake craniotomy in adult patients with DRFE. In this context, feasibility refers to the ability to complete a mapping-guided resection by reliably identifying eloquent boundaries at both cortical and subcortical levels, implying a cooperative and awake patient for effective functional brain mapping. Proper patient selection is fundamental for successful awake craniotomies, 1,16 and in our cohort, preoperative neurocognitive screening ensures exclusion of patients unable to perform intraoperative tasks. In addition, we performed the similar awake craniotomy protocol across all patients. 1,3,13,17 Nonetheless, epilepsy-specific factorssuch as seizure control, epilepsy duration, and antiseizure medication-have been previously associated with awake craniotomy failure in glioma patients. 1,18 Uncontrolled epileptic seizures are one of the five identified risk factors of intraoperative insufficient cooperation during awake craniotomy that are included in the ASIC score. 1 Here, DRFE patients of the different subgroups under study have a higher ASIC score than the control groups that did not translate into abortion of the awake procedure because of epilepsy. Contrarily, we report successful mapping in all DRFE patients, consistent with previous findings. Minkin et al. reported successful brain mapping in all cases from a series of 14 awake craniotomies in DFRE patients caused by focal cortical dysplasia. 8 Others reported low rates of unsuccessful functional mapping. Korkar et al. reported awake craniotomy abortion in 5.8% of cases 4 ; Maesawa et al. reported positive sensorimotor mapping in all but one case and positive language mapping in all but one case in a series of five awake craniotomies in DFRE patients 19 ; and Guibourd de Luzinais et al. reported one patient who did not fully awaken, leading to abortion of the procedure in a series of 22 awake craniotomies in DFRE patients. 9 Rates of delayed awakening and insufficient cooperation were low and comparable to control patients, supporting the overall feasibility of awake brain mapping in this population and the relevance of this procedure for epileptogenic lesions lying within or adjacent to eloquent brain areas.

Another concern of awake craniotomy is the occurrence of intraoperative epileptic seizures that may impact on the results of brain mapping, which may change the surgical strategy and subsequently may limit the resection. Intraoperative epileptic seizures have been reported ranging 3.4%-54.0% during awake brain mapping, leading to procedure abortion in up to 18%. 4,13,18,[20][21][22][23][24][25] To address the risk of intraoperative epileptic seizures being related to the mastery of functional brain mapping techniques, 21 we have implemented a standardized functional brain mapping protocol based on 15 years of experience in awake craniotomy, including the initial calibration at the lowest current intensity, to control for intraoperative seizures. 13 This approach enabled us to maintain low and consistent seizure rates across subgroups, without interfering with mapping completion. that the degree of seizure control and the duration of epilepsy may be a more critical determinant than the nature of the underlying lesion itself. This observation, together with the definition of the ASIC score, could help identify these patients preoperatively for counseling regarding the higher rate of intraoperative seizures. The current intensity used for functional brain was higher in the different DRFE patient subgroups, without increasing the risk of intraoperative epileptic seizures. In DRFE patients, mapping did not interfere with the procedure, suggesting that higher current thresholds safely adjusted to achieve reproducible clinical responses in these patients.

We observed a nonsignificant higher rate of early postoperative epileptic seizures across the different subgroups of patients with DRFE. This can be explained by the duration of the history of epilepsy before surgery, which is a known predictor for early postoperative epileptic seizures.

13 4.3 | Generalizability To disentangle the contribution of various clinical features in this multifactorial condition, we performed targeted subgroup analyses based on disease etiology, epilepsy duration, and the degree of drug resistance. Strengths of this study included (1) homogeneity of the cohort, which includes 558 consecutive patients who underwent the same neurosurgical procedure; (2) standardized data collection with no loss to follow-up; and (3) inclusion of a control group. These results support the safe and feasible use of awake craniotomy in carefully selected patients with DRFE, particularly when the epileptogenic zone lies close to or within eloquent brain areas. We recommend that teams aiming to implement awake craniotomy in DRFE patients first acquire comprehensive expertise in two distinct domains: conventional resective surgery for DRFE performed under general anesthesia, and awake craniotomy techniques as applied in patients with diffuse gliomas. Mastery of the specific technical nuances, indications, and potential pitfalls associated with each of these procedures is essential. Only after both skill sets are well established should these techniques be combined, ensuring that the unique challenges of awake surgery in DRFE patients can be addressed without compromising the safety or completion of the procedure.

div.head: | Limitations
div.p: Limitations include the retrospective, single-center design of the study and the lack of an external validation set. We acknowledge the heterogeneity of the LEAT and associated nontumoral epileptogenic brain lesion group, which does not share a common gene driving mutations.

We have grouped these subjects to allow statistical analyses. We acknowledge the overlaps between subgroups we analyzed to capture the different components of the epileptic disease, which may have introduced confounding effects, as several patients could meet criteria for more than one category and be incorporated into more than one subgroup. We have tried to control for this bias by using multivariable modeling. Electrocorticographic recordings were systematically performed in DRFE patients included in this study but were not routinely used in patients of the control group. Although the occurrence of intraoperative seizures was routinely identified on a clinical basis across all patients, independent of electrophysiological findings (a subclinical epileptic discharge identified on electrocorticography recording was not relevant because it did not stop the functional mapping procedure), the asymmetrical intraoperative monitoring between groups may possibly have led to increased intraoperative epileptic seizure detection in DRFE patients. We acknowledge the selection bias induced by awake craniotomy being proposed only to DRFE patients deemed amenable to perform intraoperative tasks. Nevertheless, our experience based on awake

Finally, although our findings support the feasibility and safety of awake craniotomy in this setting, the aim of the present study was not to address long-term efficacy. Such outcomes, namely, long-term seizure control and functional outcomes, remain to be evaluated on long-term cohorts.

div.head: | CO N C LUSIONS
div.p: Awake craniotomy appears to be feasible and safe in DRFE patients. In this population, the rates of adverse events, including intraoperative epileptic seizures, were low and comparable to control patients, and seizureswhen occurred-were effectively managed without compromising the surgical procedure. The present results suggest that awake craniotomy could be proposed in selected DRFE patients when the epileptogenic zone is close to or within eloquent brain areas. This could inform future prospective studies and guideline development to standardize practices in epilepsy surgery, in particular, regarding whether awake craniotomy should become the gold standard for surgical resections within eloquent brain areas.
